clinicalPearls: A non-ulcerative inflammation of the corneal stroma with intact epithelium, usually representing an immune response to a systemic infection rather than direct corneal infection
Congenital syphilis is the classic cause, typically bilateral and part of the Hutchinson triad (interstitial keratitis, notched incisors, and sensorineural deafness)
Active disease shows stromal oedema, cellular infiltration, and deep stromal vascularisation; when vessels lose their blood column they leave residual ghost vessels
Cogan syndrome links interstitial keratitis with vestibuloauditory dysfunction and may herald a systemic vasculitis
Other infective associations include tuberculosis, Lyme disease, leprosy, and herpes simplex or zoster (which more often cause unilateral disease)
Chronic sequelae include stromal scarring, thinning, and lipid keratopathy, with vision reduced by scarring and irregular astigmatism
Management combines treatment of the underlying systemic cause with topical corticosteroids to control stromal inflammation, and later keratoplasty for dense scarring
Identifying and treating the systemic cause is essential, so serological and systemic workup should accompany ocular treatment
reference.pathophysiology: Interstitial keratitis is an inflammation of the corneal stroma in which the epithelium and endothelium are typically spared and there is no primary ulceration. It usually reflects an immune (often antigen-driven or hypersensitivity) reaction to a systemic infection such as syphilis, tuberculosis, Lyme disease, or a viral agent, rather than active replication of organisms within the cornea. Inflammatory cells infiltrate the stroma, causing oedema and the ingrowth of deep stromal vessels. When inflammation subsides the vessels may empty, leaving ghost vessels, and the stroma is left scarred and sometimes thinned or laden with lipid. The resulting opacity and irregular astigmatism impair vision.
additionalDifferentials: Bacterial or fungal keratitis with stromal infiltrate
Corneal graft rejection with stromal vascularisation
Peripheral ulcerative keratitis from systemic vasculitis
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp examination documenting stromal oedema, infiltrate, and deep or ghost vessels
Tuberculosis testing (interferon-gamma release assay or tuberculin skin test and chest imaging)
Lyme serology and other targeted infective workup based on exposure history
Audiovestibular assessment when Cogan syndrome is suspected
Systemic inflammatory and vasculitis screen when an autoimmune cause is considered
redFlags: Associated vestibuloauditory symptoms suggesting Cogan syndrome and possible systemic vasculitis
Evidence of active systemic infection such as syphilis or tuberculosis requiring urgent treatment
Progressive stromal thinning with perforation risk
Dense central scarring causing significant visual loss
reference.prognosis: Active inflammation usually settles with treatment of the underlying cause and topical corticosteroids, but residual stromal scarring, ghost vessels, and irregular astigmatism can leave lasting visual impairment. Dense central scarring may ultimately require keratoplasty.
pitfalls: Treating the cornea without identifying and treating the underlying systemic infection
Missing Cogan syndrome and the risk of systemic vasculitis when hearing symptoms coexist
Confusing immune stromal inflammation with active infective keratitis
Overlooking congenital syphilis in a child with bilateral disease and systemic stigmata
references: Cornea by Krachmer, Mannis and Holland
management: Treat the underlying systemic cause, for example penicillin for syphilis or standard antitubercular therapy, rather than the cornea alone
Use topical corticosteroids to suppress stromal inflammation and limit scarring and deep vascularisation
Add a cycloplegic agent for pain relief and to prevent posterior synechiae during active inflammation
Institute systemic immunosuppression urgently for Cogan syndrome to preserve hearing
Arrange audiovestibular and systemic evaluation for associated disease such as Cogan syndrome or vasculitis
Follow up long term for residual stromal scarring, lipid keratopathy and irregular astigmatism, with keratoplasty for dense central scarring
Undertake partner notification and public health measures where an infective cause such as syphilis is confirmed
